newsitem.title: USA: Strike, incentives cut Chrysler profits 53 percent.
newsitem.headline: Strike, incentives cut Chrysler profits 53 percent.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. said Friday its second-quarter profits fell 53 percent from a year ago due to sharply higher incentive spending to lure buyers and an engine plant strike that cost it $438 million.

The profits of $483 million, or 70 cents a share, brought the high-flying No. 3 automaker back to reality, forcing it to institute austerity measures once reserved for a recession. A year earlier, Chrysler earned $1.03 billion, or $1.39 a share.

"The second quarter was a very difficult one for Chrysler," Chairman Robert Eaton said. "Our results were significantly affected by the UAW strike -- our vehicle shipments were reduced by an estimated 89,000 units."
The 29-day strike at the Mound Road engine plant in Detroit in April and May temporarily forced Chrysler to shut down seven of its 15 assembly plants in the United States, Canada and Mexico.

"While the general economy and consumer confidence continue to look good, increased competition and softer sales have forced us to increase incentives and step up our ongoing efforts to eliminate waste and reduce expenses," Eaton said.
Chrysler has put a freeze on outside hiring, is reducing overtime and travel expenses and may cut up to $1 billion in spending over the next 12 months.

The fiercely competitive U.S. car and truck market took its toll on Chrysler, forcing it to boost incentives to $980 a vehicle on average from $625 a year earlier. That figure climbed to $1,195 by the quarter's end and executives expect it to remain there while third-quarter clearance of 1997 models continues.

"Incentive levels ramped up through the quarter in an unhealthy way," said CS First Boston analyst Nicholas Colas. "But the bad news is out and we know where we stand, so we can look forward to their new product programmes."

He said Chrysler's stock, hurt recently as investors bet on weak results, has the best potential of Detroit's Big Three automakers. The stock rose 56 cents to $35.44 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

This fall, the automaker plans to introduce a new mid-size sport/utility vehicle, the Dodge Durango, a four-door Dodge Ram pickup truck and replacements for its Dodge Intrepid and Chrysler Concorde passenger cars, which analysts expect will allow Chrysler to reduce incentives.

Chrysler said its combined U.S. and Canadian market share in the second quarter fell to 15.5 percent from 16.7 percent a year earlier. But in June, after the strike was over, the company's market share had climbed back to 16.3 percent.
Sales fell to $14.4 billion from $15.8 billion but the company's credit arm, Chrysler Financial Corp., had record net income of $103 million, up from $101 million last year.

After-tax profit per vehicle in the quarter fell to $515 from $1,180 a year earlier after taking into account the engine plant strike. Excluding the strike's impact, Chrysler said it would have earned $989 per vehicle during the quarter.
Chrysler Chief Financial Officer Gary Valade likened the difficulties to a "dry run" for an industry recession because the company's shipments fell 20 percent from its planned levels for the quarter.
"It's equivalent to having a 20 percent downturn in one quarter," he said. "And we were able to react very well -- more quickly than we had anticipated."

He said Chrysler's cash reserve fell about $600 million to $7 billion in the quarter after it spent $2 billion on capital projects, stock buybacks and dividends, indicating a positive cash flow from operations.
General Motors Corp. and Ford Motor Co. are due to report earnings July 16. Ford is the only one of Detroit's Big Three expected to report higher profits.
